title: Conditioning on a total
objectives: Find chances and expectations for dice and cards given their total or their maximum.

screens.title: What is left
screens.prose: Roll two fair dice. A friend peeks and tells you the total is 8. Each cell shows the total of one of the 36 equally likely rolls.

state.caption: Rows: the first die. Columns: the second die.

screens.question: Tap every roll that is still possible.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap every cell that shows 8, and nothing else.

byKey.unordered: You counted (2, 6) but not (6, 2). They are different rolls: the first die differs.

explain.text: Five cells show 8, from (2, 6) to (6, 2). The other 31 rolls contradict what you were told, so they drop out. The five that remain are still equally likely.

screens.title: Both even?
screens.prose: The five rolls that total 8 are now the whole sample space. This is the **reduced sample space**: the condition throws out everything else, and what is left keeps equal chances.
screens.question: Given a total of 8, what is the chance both dice are even?

hints.text: Count the even pairs inside the five cells.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count inside the five shaded cells only.

byKey.unconditional: That is the chance before the condition, $\tfrac{9}{36}$. The total of 8 changes it.
byKey.unordered: You listed {2, 6}, {3, 5} and {4, 4} once each. But (2, 6) and (6, 2) are two rolls, while (4, 4) is one.

explain.text: Three of the five rolls are both even: (2, 6), (4, 4) and (6, 2). So the chance is $\tfrac35$, up from $\tfrac14$. An even total makes two odd dice or two even dice the only options.

screens.title: The larger die
screens.prose: Now each cell shows the larger of the two dice. You are told the total is 10.

state.caption: Cells show the larger die. Shaded: total 10.

screens.question: Given a total of 10, what is the expected larger die? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Read the larger die in each shaded cell.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the larger die over the three shaded cells.

byKey.each-die: That is the mean of either die, $\tfrac{10}{2}$. The larger die is at least that.
byKey.unordered: You averaged {4, 6} and {5, 5} once each. (4, 6) and (6, 4) are two rolls.
byKey.unconditional: That is the larger die with no condition, $\tfrac{161}{36}$.

explain.text: Three rolls total 10, and their larger dice are 6, 5 and 6. The mean is $\tfrac{17}{3} \approx 5.67$. A conditional mean is an average over the reduced sample space.

screens.title: Given the maximum
screens.prose: A twist: you are told the larger die is 5, not the total. The cells still show the larger die.
screens.question: Tap every roll whose larger die is 5.

hints.text: They form an L: row 5 and column 5, up to (5, 5).
5 in row 5 plus 4 more in column 5: nine cells.

feedback.correct: Nine rolls: an L of $2 \times 5 - 1$ cells.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap every cell that shows 5.

byKey.cross: You took all of row 5 and column 5. (5, 6) and (6, 5) have larger die 6.
byKey.row: You fixed the first die at 5. The second die can be the 5 instead.

explain.text: The larger die is 5 when one die is 5 and the other at most 5. That is row 5 and column 5 up to (5, 5): $2 \times 5 - 1 = 9$ cells. The corner (5, 5) is one roll, not two.

screens.title: The other die is still fair?
screens.prose: Given that the larger die is 5, a candidate says: one die is a 5, and the other is fair. So both are 5 with chance $\tfrac16$.
screens.question: Given the larger die is 5, what is the chance both dice are 5?

options.why: You kept the other die uniform. The condition changes it: (5, 5) is one cell of nine.
You listed the other die as 1 to 5, equally likely. But (5, 2) and (2, 5) are two cells, while (5, 5) is one.
That is the chance before the condition.

hints.text: The L has nine equally likely cells.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells of the L and the cells where both are 5.

byKey.b: You treated the other die as still fair. Given the maximum, the other die is not uniform.
byKey.c: You split the other die evenly over 1 to 5. A 5 alongside is one roll; a 2 alongside is two.

explain.text: Nine rolls have larger die 5, and only (5, 5) has both. So the chance is $\tfrac19$. The other die is not fair after the condition: it is 5 in one cell of nine.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Each answer kept only the rolls that agree with the condition $B$, each still equally likely, and counted inside them:

$$P(A \mid B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|B|}, \qquad E[X \mid B] = \frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{\omega \in B} X(\omega).$$
screens.question: Given that two dice total 12, what is the chance both show 6?

options.why: That is before the condition. A total of 12 leaves one roll.
You kept one die uniform. A total of 12 forces both dice.

feedback.correct: 1: a total of 12 leaves nothing uncertain.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many rolls total 12?

explain.text: The edge case: a total of 2 or 12 leaves one roll. Then every conditional chance is 0 or 1.

screens.title: The expected total
screens.prose: Given the larger die is 5, find the expected total. Put the working in order, one justified line at a time.

state.caption: Cells show the total. Shaded: larger die 5.

screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: The rolls with larger die 5 are $(5, b)$ for $b \le 5$ and $(a, 5)$ for $a \le 4$.
The rolls $(5, b)$ have totals 6 to 10, which add to 40.
The rolls $(a, 5)$ have totals 6 to 9, which add to 30.
Each die is uniform on 1 to 5, so the expected total is 6.
lines.why: The condition is not "both at most 5". One die must be a 5.

hints.text: List the rolls in the L first.
Split the L into its row and its column, without counting (5, 5) twice.
Rolls, count, two partial sums, mean.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin by listing the rolls in the L.

byKey.d1: You treated both dice as uniform on 1 to 5. One of them is 5 for certain.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the uniform claim belongs.

explain.text: The row gives totals 6 to 10 (sum 40) and the column gives 6 to 9 (sum 30). Over nine rolls the mean is $\tfrac{70}{9} \approx 7.78$. Without the condition it would be 7.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `conditional(event, given, n_dice=2, faces=6)`. List every roll and keep those where `given(roll)` is true. Return the share where `event(roll)` is true, as a `Fraction`. Then write `cond_mean(f, given, ...)`, the average of `f(roll)` over the kept rolls.
screens.question: Write both functions.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction
from itertools import product


def conditional(event, given, n_dice=2, faces=6):
    """P(event | given) over every equally likely roll, exact."""
    rolls = list(product(range(1, faces + 1), repeat=n_dice))
    ...


def cond_mean(f, given, n_dice=2, faces=6):
    """E[f(roll) | given], exact."""
    ...

examples.call: conditional(lambda r: r[0] % 2 == 0 and r[1] % 2 == 0, lambda r: sum(r) == 8)

tests.call: conditional(lambda r: r[0] % 2 == 0 and r[1] % 2 == 0, lambda r: sum(r) == 8)
conditional(lambda r: r == (5, 5), lambda r: max(r) == 5)
conditional(lambda r: 1 in r, lambda r: sum(r) == 6)
conditional(lambda r: 3 in r, lambda r: sum(r) == 5, n_dice=3)
conditional(lambda r: 6 in r, lambda r: sum(r) == 7)

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests, each an exact `Fraction`: five chances and four conditional means. One uses three dice and one ten-sided dice.

hints.text: Filter first: `kept = [r for r in rolls if given(r)]`.
`Fraction(count, len(kept))` for a chance; `Fraction(sum(f(r) for r in kept), len(kept))` for a mean.

feedback.correct: Filter, then count: the reduced sample space in code.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Divide by the number of kept rolls, not by all 36.
byKey.test-6: Average `f` over the kept rolls only.

explain.text: The filter is the condition and the count is the event. With 36 or 216 rolls, enumeration is instant and exact. Ten-sided dice with total 11 give a mean larger die of 8.

screens.title: Drill: three more
screens.prose: Drill: about 3 minutes a puzzle, as interviews allow. Keep your own time and say each argument aloud. Give four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: Two dice total 6. The chance at least one die shows 1?
The larger of two dice is 6. The expected smaller die?
Three dice total 5. The chance one of them shows 3?

hints.text: List the rolls that meet each condition.
Total 6: five rolls. Larger 6: eleven rolls. Three dice total 5: six rolls.
$\tfrac25$; then $\tfrac{21 + 15}{11}$; then (1, 1, 3) in three orders out of six.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Check the first: (1, 5) and (5, 1) of five rolls.
byKey.r1c1: Check the second: the smaller dice are 1 to 6 in row 6 and 1 to 5 in column 6.
byKey.r2c1: Check the third: (1, 1, 3) and (1, 2, 2) each come in three orders.

explain.text: Total 6 leaves five rolls, two with a 1. Larger 6 leaves eleven rolls whose smaller dice add to 36. Three dice total 5 in six ways, three of them with a 3.

screens.title: Drill: a six?
screens.prose: One more at the same pace. Two dice total 7.
screens.question: What is the chance that one of the dice shows a six?

options.why: That is the chance of a six with no condition. The total of 7 changes it.
You kept one die uniform. Either die can be the six, and the condition reshapes both.
You split "a six" and "no six" as if equally likely. Count the six rolls.

hints.text: Two of them hold a six.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the rolls with total 7 that include a six.

byKey.b: You used the chance before the condition.
byKey.c: You treated one die as still fair. Count the six rolls instead.

explain.text: Six rolls total 7, and (1, 6) and (6, 1) hold a six. So the chance is $\tfrac13$, a little above $\tfrac{11}{36}$.

screens.title: Follow-up: $n$-sided dice
screens.prose: The interviewer extends it: two fair $n$-sided dice total $n + 1$. What is the expected larger die? Work out two cases, then spot the pattern.
screens.question: Fill in the expected larger die.

hints.text: Total $n + 1$ gives the rolls $(a, n + 1 - a)$ for $a = 1$ to $n$.
Each value from $\tfrac{n}{2} + 1$ to $n$ appears twice, so the mean is $\tfrac{3n + 2}{4}$ for even $n$.

feedback.correct: 5, 8 and 75.5: the mean is $\tfrac{3n + 2}{4}$ for even $n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r2c1: Check the pattern: the values 51 to 100, each twice.

explain.text: The larger die runs over the top half of the faces, each value twice. Its mean is the middle of $\tfrac{n}{2} + 1$ and $n$, which is $\tfrac{3n + 2}{4}$. That gives 5, 8 and 75.5; check it against the case you counted before trusting it.

screens.title: A two-day P&L
screens.prose: A strategy's daily P&L is one of $-2, -1, 0, +1$ or $+2$, in £k. Each is equally likely, independently of other days. Its two-day total was $+1$.

state.caption: Cells show the two-day total in £k.

screens.question: Given the total, what is the chance the strategy had a losing day?

hints.text: Two of the four include a losing day.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count inside the four cells with total +1.

byKey.unconditional: That is the chance with no condition, $1 - (\tfrac35)^2$.
byKey.none: A positive total does not rule out a loss: (−1, +2) is possible.

explain.text: Four day pairs total $+1$, and two of them hold a losing day. So the chance is $\tfrac12$, below the unconditional 0.64. A total of $+2$, by contrast, rules out any losing day.

ideas: A condition keeps only the outcomes that agree with it, and those keep equal chances.
Count the event inside the condition, or average the quantity over it.
After conditioning on a total or a maximum, the dice are no longer independent. Given the maximum, the other die is not even uniform.

formula.name: Counting inside the condition
formula.note: Ordered rolls: (2, 6) and (6, 2) are two outcomes; (4, 4) is one.

summary.trap: Treating the other die as still fair. Given the larger die is 5, both are 5 with chance $\tfrac19$, not $\tfrac16$.

quiz.prose: Two cards are drawn from a shuffled deck. You learn they are the same colour.
quiz.question: What is the chance both are hearts? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the same-colour pairs, then the heart pairs among them.

byKey.unconditional: That is the chance before the condition, $\tfrac{78}{1326}$.
byKey.half: You took $\tfrac12 \times \tfrac12$ for two hearts among red pairs. Red pairs are only half the same-colour pairs.

explain.text: There are $2\binom{26}{2} = 650$ same-colour pairs and $\binom{13}{2} = 78$ heart pairs. So the chance is $\tfrac{78}{650} = \tfrac{3}{25}$.

quiz.question: What is the chance they show a double?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the five rolls that total 8.

byKey.unconditional: That is the chance of a double with no condition.
byKey.unordered: You counted {2, 6}, {3, 5} and {4, 4} once each. There are five ordered rolls.

explain.text: Five rolls total 8, and only (4, 4) is a double. So the chance is $\tfrac15$.

quiz.question: What is the expected value of the first die?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. By symmetry, the two dice share the total.

byKey.unconditional: That is the mean with no condition. A total of 9 pushes both dice up.

explain.text: The rolls (3, 6), (4, 5), (5, 4) and (6, 3) total 9. By symmetry each die averages half the total, $\tfrac92$.
